opus-5.5.text:
Ha, that's a fun question, because the names often don't tell you much. At Tsinghua, a lot of department names carry history. They were set up decades ago, when the country needed engineers for very specific things, and the names stuck even as the actual research moved on.

Take Electronic Engineering. If you just read the name, you'd picture circuits, radios, maybe signal processing. Those foundations are still there. But when I was a student, a lot of the energy in the department was going into information theory, communications, and more and more into computer vision and machine learning. Many people in EE ended up doing what you'd honestly call AI research. Meanwhile, Computer Science and Technology also does AI, and Automation, which sounds like factory control systems, does a huge amount of robotics, pattern recognition, and intelligent systems. So you have three or four departments whose names suggest quite different things, all converging on very similar problems.

I think that says something about how fields evolve. The names reflect the boundaries of the problems people were solving fifty years ago. Research doesn't respect those boundaries for long. A good problem, like getting a machine to see, understand, and act in the physical world, pulls in signal processing, control, computing, and mechanics all at once.

For students this can be confusing. A high schooler picks a major based on the name and then discovers the real content is something else. But it can also be an advantage. You get a different set of foundational training depending on where you start. An EE person thinks about signals and noise. An automation person thinks about feedback and control. A CS person thinks about algorithms and systems. When those people meet on the same problem, that's often where interesting work happens.

So my short answer is that the names tell you where a department came from, not necessarily where it's going. If you want to know what a department really studies, look at what the young faculty and the PhD students are working on right now. That's the real signal.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, because it's one of those things you don't notice until you leave and come back. At Tsinghua the names are often historical artifacts more than descriptions. Take the Department of Automation, which is where I spent a lot of time. "Automation" sounds like factory robots, and that was the founding spirit in the 1970s. But by the time I was there, people were doing control theory, machine learning, computer vision, even bioinformatics. If you walked into a lab expecting assembly lines, you'd be confused.

The same thing happens with "Electronic Engineering" versus "Computer Science." On paper there's a clean split. In practice, half the EE students are writing deep learning code and half the CS students are worrying about hardware. The name tells you about the lineage of the department, who founded it, what the national priorities were when it was set up. It tells you much less about what a given professor is actually doing today.

I actually think that's fine, and even a little healthy. If you renamed every department to match its current research, you'd be renaming them every five years. What matters more is the culture underneath. Automation had this engineering mindset: build the system, make it work end to end, don't just prove a theorem. That carried into how I approached research in the US and later in robotics. So the name was wrong in the literal sense but right in the deeper sense, if that makes any sense.

r001.rationale: The response says department names are often historical artifacts and tell much less about current research, which conveys that many names do not reflect their principal research directions.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify mechanical engineering as a traditional stronghold of robotics.

r003.rationale: It mentions control theory as research in Automation, but does not identify control as a traditional stronghold of robotics.
